Sultan Ahmed, D.A.G. with Sajjad Ali Chowdhury ------ For the State.

full_judgment:
[The evidence of the witnesses and their discussion by the court is unnecessary for reporting and therefore omitted.] 

 5. PW 9 Osman Gani is a witness who attested Seizure list (Ext 2). In his presence blood stained earth and other alamats were seized. His evidence has been assailed on the ground that seizure list does not bear his signature and that seizure of alamats was not made in accordance with law. This witness deposed on oath that alamats were seized in his presence and a seizure list was prepared at the place of occurrence. In the order sheet it has been noted that alamats marked Ext VI series were produced in the Court during trial (vide order No. 30 dated 29-8-84). Absence of the signature in the seizure list of the witness may be due to accidental omission. The learned counsel for the defence has made a grievance that seizure of alamats was not made in accordance with legal procedure and as such the seizure list (Ext 2) should be left out of consideration. According to learned lawyer's contention, alamats ought to have been seized in presence of respectable persons of the locality and since seizure list was not prepared in presence of respectable persons of locality, the conviction cannot be sustained. In support of this contention, reliance was placed in the decision reported in 26 DLR (1974) 297. Facts involved in the cited case is distinguishable from the facts of the instant case. In the cited case search was conducted to find out arms from the house of the accused and so their Lordships enunciated the principle that while conducting search, procedure laid down in section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure should be strictly complied with. The requirement of law in that regard is that two respectable men of the locality are to he made present at the time of search and this measure has been made imperative to guard against implanting arms secretly without the knowledge of accused and thereby to implicate him in a false case. The procedure laid down in section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not required to be followed at the time of seizure of alamats by the investigating officer. Any person present at the time of seizing alamats can be made witness to the seizure list. Law does not require that respectable men of the locality have to be made witnesses in the seizure list. Procedure followed while conducting search as per provision of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is different from procedure followed by investigating Officer while seizing alamats during Investigation. Investigating Officer is required to go to the place of occurrence and to seize alamats which are connected with occurrence in presence of some persons present there. Procedure of search under section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and that of seizure of alamats at place of occurrence by Investigating Officer, stand altogether in different footing. 

 Evidence of PW 10 Dr Nripendra Nath Roy who conducted autopsy on the dead body of deceased Amjad Hossain has already been referred hence before. So no need of reiterating his evidence here. 

 6. The learned counsel has made grievance that all the witness examined in this case by the prosecution side are interested being relation of the deceased Amjad and as such their testimony should not be acted upon without corroboration from independent source on all material points. It is true that all the witnesses except PW 6 Joynal are related to the deceased Amjad Hossain. But it has been found that PW 1 Nuruzzaman, PW 6 Nurun Nahar and PW 3 Tosoruddin are the eye-witnesses to the occurrence. A close relative who is very natural witness cannot be branded an interested witness. The word "interested" postulates that witness must have some direct interest in having the accused somehow or other convicted for some animus or for other reasons. Interested witness is not necessarily false witness though in fact that witness has personal interest in the matter. Evidence of such witness should be scrutinised on its merit, before investigating whether witness is interested one and such scrutiny of evidence is required as rule of prudence and not as rule of law. In the instant case eye-witnesses have no direct interest in securing punishment of the appellants by giving false evidence. Defence side did not impute any animus to those witnesses. 

 7. Minor discrepancy in human testimony is bound to occur. Oral evidence dependent on such inconsistent factor as human nature cannot be reduced to set formulae. Further close relation will be the last person to screen the real culprit and falsely implicate an innocent person. Hence relationship far from being foundation of criticism of defence is often guarantee of its truth. No doubt no sweeping generalisation can be possible in all cases. At the same time there cannot be general rule of prudence to require corroboration before the evidence is believed. In fact, question of relationship of witness to the deceased comes up practically in every criminal case and court is to deal with this aspect of the matter more often. Now it is consistent view of the superior courts that relationship per se of witnesses is not sufficient to discredit the testimony of witness specially who are eye-witness if the same is otherwise corroborated, by circumstances attending the occurrence. 

 8. The next contention urged by the learned counsel for the defence is that in the instant case there is no motive on the part of the appellants to murder deceased Amjad Hossain inasmuch as appellants had no strained relation or ill feeling with deceased. True, no evidence is forthcoming in this case to prove, motive behind this murder. But prosecution is not bound to prove motive, only the culprit knows what facts influence to move him to action. Proof of motive or previous ill feeling is not necessary to sustain conviction when court is satisfied that appellants are assailants of the victim. When positive evidence against the accused is clear, cogent and reliable motive is of no importance. Failure to prove motive does not throw overboard the entire prosecution case. It only casts duty on court to scrutinise evidence particularly of eye-witnesses with great care. So absence of proof of motive cannot affect merit of the case. Another grievance has been made by the learned counsel for the defence that many disinterested persons from neighbour hood came to the place of occurrence but none of them has been examined in this case. True many persons from the locality came to the place of occurrence but there is no hard and fast rule as to number of witnesses to be examined by prosecution. Court is to see if witnesses examined are trustworthy and independent witnesses and implicit belief can be placed on their testimony. The learned counsel for the defence has made another grievance that examination of the appellants under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not done in accordance with law. He has submitted in this connection that incriminating evidence transpired against each of the appellants was not brought to his notice and thereby the very object of law envisaged in section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has been frustrated. It is further submitted by the learned counsel that mere asking "you have heard the evidence; what is reply, and in reply appellant said I am innocent."This sort of examination in question and answer form cannot be treated to be proper compliance of the provisions of section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In reply to this contention the learned Deputy Attorney General submitted that though each appellant was asked in question and answer form that cannot be treated to be a gross irregularity vitiating trial and to support this contention he referred the decision in the case of Abdul Wahab vs The Crown reported in 7 D LR 87. In that case examination of the accused under section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code was made in question and answer form as indicated above. Their Lordships observed in the following words: — 

 9. Their Lordships having reviewed number of decisions touching on the point held that failure to draw the incriminating evidence to the notice of accused while being examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be an irregularity and if no miscarriage of justice is occasioned because of such irregularity, it is curable by section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In the instant case no evidence has been brought on record to show that for want of proper and strict compliance of provision of section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure there has been failure of justice. So non-compliance of provision of the Code of Criminal Procedure strictly may be an irregularity and it is curable under section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 10. Another contention urged by the learned Counsel for the defence side is that evidence recorded by the trial Court was not read over and explained to each witness and this irregularity is not curable by section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and it has vitiated the trial. This contention being devoid of substance is also not tenable in law. On scrutiny of the record it appears that each witness put his or her signature on the deposition sheet wherein evidence was recorded. It is through oversight that seal of the Court reading "interpreted, explained and admitted to be correct." was not put below signature of each witness. When witnesses put .the signature in the exposition sheet, it can reasonably be presumed that witnesses being conversant with contents and meaning of evidence put signature in the deposition sheet. So from this fact it can be inferred that deposition was read over to the witnesses who being satisfied about correctness of recording of evidence put signature on it. Further, even if it is assumed for argument's sake that evidence was not read over, such omission constitutes an irregularity which is curable under section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In this connection the decision in the case of Shabitri Bala Shar versus Shaha Muhammad Ashaque Munshi reported in (1956) 8 DLR 154, PLD 1957 Dacca 127 may be referred. In that case also similar irregularity occurred. His Lordships observed in the following terms:— 

 "Non-compliance with provisions of section 360 whether the mere irregularity curable under section 537 question whether deposition had been, duly read over and explained to witnesses under what circumstances requires to be raised by person complaining of non-compliance, expressly upon an affidavit showing in what material respect the omission had prejudiced him—Evidence Act (I of 1972)". 

 11. All the appellants made preparation to commit the murder. In popular sense assembling to commit murder may be act of preparation. All the eye-witnesses as well as other witnesses made uniform statement in their respective evidence that all the 14 appellants except appellant Mojibar being armed with deadly weapons like dagger, bollom, lathi remained hidden in a paddy field and they emerged from their hiding place to attack the victim when appellant Mojibar grappled him from behind and felled him to the ground. Further appellant Majibar was sent to the victim Amjad Hossain on the pretext of asking for medicine knowing fully well that he had no medicine with him. The object of sending the appellant Mojibar in advance was to prevent the victim to escape assault by running away. This act of having remained hidden in a paddy field being armed with deadly weapons and suddenly emerging out from the place on opportune moment and carrying out assault on the victim, demonstrates clearly the intention of the appellants to kill the victim. It can be said that all the appellants shared the common intention of murdering the victim, in furtherance of common intention of all. In fact, all appellants joined together and abetted each other in commission of the act although some appellants may net assault victim with their own hand. 

 12. In this case First Information Report was lodged by P W 1 Nuruzzaman promptly that is, within 4 hours of the occurrence. The thana is 9 miles away from the place of occurrence. So there is no manner of doubt that the incident was reported to the thana with maximum promptitude. It is a settled law that where accused persons are named in promptly lodged report and version disclosed therein is supported by medical evidence which is to be discussed in appropriate place, it would not be necessary to look for corroboration and the rest of evidence available on record will be enough to bring home the guilt to the accused person. So in the instant case the promptly lodged FIR is a fact which goes against the appellants. 

 13. Specific conduct of the appellants also speak against them. Charge sheet in this case was filed showing the appellants absconding. Two appellants were tried in absentia. Failure to put forward any explanation of abscondance after occurrence is a point in favour of prosecution. Presence of eye-witnesses, namely, PW 1 Nuruzzaman, PW 2 Nurun Nahar and PW 3 Tosoruddin at the place of occurrence has been proved beyond doubt. Evidence on this point is over whelming and is unchallenged. 

 14. Now it is to be seen if medical evidence corroborates the ocular evidence Medical evidence as it appears from the deposition of PW 10 Nripendra Nath Roy, the deceased Amjad Hossain sustained as many as 7 injuries all of which are incised except injury No. 2 which has been found by the Doctor to be lacerated. Eye-witness PW 1 Nuruzzaman, P,W 2 Nurun Nahar and PW 3 Toseruddin uniformly stated in their evidence that victim Amjad Hossain sustained incised injury on the right shoulder, on the right hand which resulted in severance of the four fingers of the victim from the hand (injury No. 5) and other incised injury on the chest (injury No, 6). Thus it appears that the type of weapons used in causing three injuries fully lend corroborative support to ocular evidence of PW 1 Nuruzzaman, PW 2 Nurun Nahar and PW 3 Toseruddin, of course discrepancy occurred in respect of the name of the appellant responsible for causing of those three injuries. The discrepancy in respect of the name of the assailants of those injuries can be overlooked, in view of the fact that ocular evidence in this regard finds full support from medical evidence. 

 15. So far injury No. 2 is concerned, it is found to be lacerated one and it is found to be inconsistent with ocular evidence inasmuch as ocular evidence does not speak of lacerated injury. But evidence on records shows that some of the appellants were armed with lathi. So injury No. 2 being caused by some appellants cannot be ruled out. Site of injury No. 2 is on the right side of the ear of the victim and injury No. 3 which is on the shoulder is also on the right side. So ocular and medical evidence regarding the site of the injury is consistent. The gap between injury No. 2-3, that is, ear and right shoulder is very narrow. So witness might have been confused in identifying the actual location of injury No. 2. Thus medical evidence relating to site of injury on the body of the victim Amjad and nature of weapon used in causing injury Nos. 3 ,5, and 6 find complete support from medical evidence. Under this circumstances we are unerringly of opinion that ocular evidence stands fully corroborated by medical evidence. 

 Thus having considered the entire evidence on record, facts and circumstances and probability of the case and that ocular evidence of the aforesaid eye-witnesses being fully corroborated by medical evidence referred above, we are unerringly of opinion that guilt has been brought home to each of the appellant. 

 16. Now let us turn to the defence version. Defence side has examined the witnesses. DW 1 Nasimuddin and DW 2 Voula. According to defence version the deceased Amjad Hossain was killed by some unknown miscreants in the previous night. But the evidence of these two defence witnesses does not in any way support the defence contention. From their evidence it is not clear where the murder of deceased Amjad Hossain took place. Mere suggestion that some miscreants killed him in the previous night cannot outweigh overwhelming evidence led by prosecution to prove that murder took place at about 4 pm on 16th Kartick on Monday at the pathway running in paddy field. The sketch map (Ext 3) prepared by the Investigation Officer and the fact of seizure of blood stained earth and blood stained wearing apparel of the victim pinpoint the place of occurrence. This evidence unmistakenably shows that occurrence took place at the pathway as shown in the sketch map Ext A and on the date and time as mentioned by the prosecution side.
